headline: Why Matrix Multiplication Is Really Just Composing Transformations
lede: The standard formula for matrix multiplication — where each entry is a row-dot-column sum — is technically correct but offers no hint of why the operation is defined that way. Tivadar Danka, a Hungarian PhD mathematician who publishes the newsletter *The Palindrome*, argues that the simple explanation lies in thinking of matrices not as grids of numbers but as encodings of geometric transformations. Once that reframing takes hold, the multiplication rule need not be memorized; it can be derived.
body:
The standard definition of matrix multiplication states that entry (AB)ᵢⱼ equals the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. It is computationally reliable and examinations require it, but it explains nothing. Students learn the recipe and pass the test; the underlying logic remains hidden.

The key realization is that **matrices are not grids of numbers but representations of *linear transformations*** — mappings between vector spaces that preserve addition and scalar multiplication. Any such transformation is completely determined by where it sends the *standard basis vectors* (e₁, e₂, ..., eₙ — the unit vectors pointing along each coordinate axis). Any input vector can be written as a weighted sum of those basis vectors; linearity guarantees the output is the same weighted sum of their images. Those images, placed side by side as columns, constitute the matrix. The j-th column of A is precisely where eⱼ lands.

Matrix-vector multiplication then follows without ceremony: **Ax is a *linear combination* of A's columns**, weighted by the coordinates of x. Matrix-matrix multiplication becomes an exercise in function *composition*. To compute AB, ask where the combined operation — apply B first, then apply A — sends each basis vector. B carries eⱼ to the j-th column of B; A then acts on that result. Column j of AB is therefore A times column j of B. Stack those outputs and C = AB materializes without any row-dot-column arithmetic.

This reframing resolves several puzzles that the formula-first approach leaves hanging. **Non-commutativity** — the fact that AB ≠ BA in general — becomes obvious: function composition is order-dependent, just as rotating then shearing a plane differs from shearing then rotating. Associativity holds because function composition is always associative. The identity matrix sends every basis vector to itself, exactly as an identity function should. The matrix inverse is simply the inverse transformation.

Danka is the author of *Mathematics of Machine Learning* (Packt Publishing) and writes *The Palindrome*, a Substack newsletter with tens of thousands of subscribers. The basis-vector view he champions is not new — it underpins Grant Sanderson's acclaimed *Essence of Linear Algebra* video series on YouTube and Gilbert Strang's MIT OpenCourseWare lectures, which anchor instruction in the 'column picture' of matrix operations from the first lecture. What the thread does well is compress a genuinely liberating insight into a format that travels: the standard formula is not arbitrary; it is the coordinate-level bookkeeping of something far more elegant.

concepts.definition: A mapping between vector spaces that preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication. Geometrically, it keeps grid lines parallel and evenly spaced while leaving the origin fixed. Every matrix encodes exactly one linear transformation, and every linear transformation between finite-dimensional spaces can be written as a matrix.

The set of unit vectors that point along each coordinate axis: e₁ = (1,0,...,0), e₂ = (0,1,...,0), and so on. Any vector in the space can be expressed as a weighted sum of them, making them a minimal skeleton that fully determines what a linear transformation does to every possible input. The columns of a matrix are precisely the images of these basis vectors.

A sum of vectors each multiplied by a scalar (a plain number). For example, 3·v₁ + 5·v₂ is a linear combination of v₁ and v₂. The column view of matrix multiplication rests on the fact that Ax equals a linear combination of A's columns, with the entries of x as the scalar weights — a far more intuitive framing than the row-dot-column calculation.

Applying one function to the output of another. If f and g are functions, their composition f∘g means 'apply g first, then apply f.' Matrix multiplication AB encodes exactly this: B is applied first, then A acts on the result. The right-to-left reading order of AB mirrors standard mathematical function-composition notation.

A property of an operation where swapping the order of inputs changes the result. Matrix multiplication is non-commutative: AB and BA generally differ, and one may not even be defined. This follows naturally from the fact that composing transformations is order-dependent — the sequence in which you apply them matters.

An interpretive lens on matrix operations that reads each column of a matrix as the image of the corresponding basis vector under the transformation the matrix represents. Under this view, multiplying two matrices means computing where each basis vector lands after successive transformations, rather than grinding through row-dot-column arithmetic. Pedagogues such as Gilbert Strang and Grant Sanderson have made this the preferred starting point for teaching linear algebra.

books.title: Mathematics of Machine Learning
books.author: Tivadar Danka
books.summary: A textbook published by Packt Publishing covering the core mathematical disciplines — linear algebra, calculus, and probability — needed to understand machine learning rigorously. Danka wrote it to bridge the gap between practitioners who can run models and those who understand why the models behave as they do. It reflects the pedagogical philosophy of *The Palindrome*: intuition before formalism, geometry before formula.
